title: Activities of U.S. Multinational Enterprises, 2024
body: News Release Explore Product View News Release Related Materials Contacts EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 8:30 a.m. EST, Friday, November 20, 2026 BEA 26–49 Activities of U.S. Multinational Enterprises, 2024 Worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises increased 0.9 percent to 44.2 million workers in 2024 (preliminary) from 43.8 million workers in 2023 (revised), according to statistics released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis on the operations and finances of U.S. parent companies and their majority-owned foreign affiliates. Employment in the United States by U.S. parents increased 0.1 percent to 29.9 million workers in 2024. U.S. parents accounted for 67.6 percent of worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises (MNEs), down from 68.1 percent in 2023. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates of U.S. MNEs increased 2.7 percent to 14.3 million workers and accounted for 32.4 percent of employment by U.S. MNEs worldwide. U.S. parents accounted for 21.7 percent of total private industry employment in the United States in 2024, down from 21.9 percent in 2023. Employment by U.S. parents was largest in manufacturing, in “other industries,” led by transportation and warehousing, and in retail trade. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates was largest in India, Mexico, and the United Kingdom. Worldwide current-dollar value added of U.S. MNEs increased 8.0 percent to $7.4 trillion in 2024. Value added by U.S. parents , a measure of U.S. parents’ direct contribution to U.S. gross domestic product, increased 8.5 percent to $5.7 trillion. U.S parents accounted for 21.8 percent of total U.S. private-industry value added, up from 21.2 percent in 2023. Foreign affiliate value added increased 6.5 percent to $1.8 trillion. Value added by foreign affiliates was largest in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Canada. Worldwide expenditures for property, plant, and equipment of U.S. MNEs increased 7.1 percent to $1.2 trillion. Expenditures by U.S. parents accounted for $968.7 billion, representing 36.5 percent of all U.S. private-business capital expenditures. Expenditures by foreign affiliates accounted for $216.2 billion. Worldwide research and development (R&D) expenditures of U.S. MNEs increased 10.1 percent to $622.7 billion. U.S. parents accounted for expenditures of $536.5 billion, representing 69.6 percent of business R&D performed in the United States. Foreign affiliates accounted for expenditures of $86.2 billion. Additional statistics on the activities of U.S. parent companies and their foreign affiliates , including sales, balance sheet and income statement items, compensation of employees, trade in goods, and more are available on BEA’s website. More industry detail for U.S. parents and more industry and country detail for foreign affiliates are also available on the website. Updates to the statistics Statistics for 2023 were revised to incorporate newly available and revised source data. Preliminary statistics for 2023 were released in August 2025. Updates to Statistics on 2023 Activities of U.S. Multinational Enterprises [Billions of dollars, except as noted] U.S. parents Majority-owned foreign affiliates Preliminary estimate Revised estimate Preliminary estimate Revised estimate Number of employees (thousands) 29,890.6 29,841.8 14,008.4 13,958.5 Value added 5,265.5 5,245.4 1,645.6 1,648.4 Expenditures for property, plant, and equipment 886.1 891.9 216.2 214.0 Research and development expenditures 476.6 481.5 81.7 84.1 U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis Related Data Tables For the 2024 activities of U.S. multinational enterprises statistics highlighted in this release, as well as estimates for earlier years, see the below data tables in BEA’s Interactive Data Application and comprehensive data tables . Selected data Selected Financial and Operating Data of U.S. Parents, by Industry of U.S. Parent Selected Data for Foreign Affiliates and U.S. Parents in All Industries Employment U.S. Parent Companies Employment, by Industry of U.S. Parent Company Foreign Affiliates Employment, by Country Foreign Affiliates Employment, by Industry of Affiliate Foreign Affiliates Employment, by Country and Industry Value added U.S. Parent Companies Value Added, by Industry of U.S. Parent Company Foreign Affiliates Value Added, by Country Foreign Affiliates Value Added, by Industry of Affiliate Expenditures for property, plant, and equipment (capital expenditures) U.S. Parent Companies Capital Expenditures, by Industry of U.S. Parent Company Foreign Affiliates Capital Expenditures, by Country Foreign Affiliates Capital Expenditures, by Industry of Affiliate R&D expenditures U.S. Parent Companies R&D Expenditures, by Industry of U.S. Parent Company Foreign Affiliates R&D Expenditures, by Country Foreign Affiliates R&D Expenditures, by Industry of Affiliate Notes. This release includes, for the first time, statistics on U.S. parent shares of domestic activity for R&D performed and for property, plant, and equipment expenditures. BEA has updated its disclosure avoidance method to coarsening, which includes rounding, aggregation, and the use of ranges. This allows BEA to publish more data while still providing confidentiality to BEA’s survey respondents. For resources, definitions, statistical conventions, and more, visit " Additional Information ." title: ADA Settlement Requires Accessibility Improvements at Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department
body: Press Release ADA Settlement Requires Accessibility Improvements at Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Middle District of Georgia Facility to Make Accessibility Improvements to Soccer Fields, Parking, and Restrooms MACON, Ga. – The Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department has agreed to make accessibility improvements across its facility following an investigation by the U.S. Attorney's Office into allegations that certain areas were not readily accessible to or usable by individuals with disabilities, as required by the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). “We appreciate the cooperation shown by the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department in addressing these concerns and taking the necessary steps to improve accessibility,” said U.S. Attorney William R. “Will” Keyes. “When individuals and families raise concerns about barriers for people with disabilities, they help improve access for the entire community. The Americans with Disabilities Act plays a vital role in ensuring equal opportunity, and this agreement will help all members of the community fully access and enjoy the department's programs, services, and amenities.” The investigation was initiated by the U.S. Attorney’s Office after receiving a complaint from a family with multiple children with disabilities. The family frequently used the facility and services offered at 250 West Dykes Street, Cochran, Georgia, and reported that the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department did not provide adequate accessible parking; accessible restroom facilities; safe, stable walking surfaces to and from the restroom; and did not provide wheelchair access to several playing fields or any of the five soccer fields located within the 28-acre facility, all in violation of the ADA. Under the Letter of Resolution signed on Nov. 18, the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department has agreed to complete the following improvements: By Feb. 15, 2027, the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department will: Create the required number and type of designated accessible parking spaces; Construct an accessible restroom within the main concession building and install directional signage throughout the facility identifying its location; and Provide accessible routes connecting the soccer complex to the accessible restroom. By July 1, 2028, the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department will: Create an accessible route from the facility entrance through the soccer field complex, connecting to other athletic fields and the accessible restroom; and Create, improve, or repair accessible routes connecting facility entrances to playing fields, play areas, restrooms, and picnic shelters. Under federal law, discrimination based on disability in the services, facilities, privileges, advantages, or accommodations provided by entities such as the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department is prohibited. Public facilities are required to comply with the ADA's accessibility standards and must be readily accessible to and usable by individuals with disabilities, including those who use wheelchairs and other mobility devices. ADA complaints may be made by contacting the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Georgia at (478) 752-3511. The investigation and resolution of this matter were led by Civil Rights Investigative Specialist Danyelle D. White, Civil Chief Bernard Snell, Assistant U.S. Attorney Hannah Couch, and former Assistant U.S. Attorney Lance Simon of the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Georgia, in coordination with the Disability Rights Section of the U.S. Department of Justice's Civil Rights Division. Updated November 20, 2026 Topics Civil Rights Disability Rights Components Civil Rights Division USAO - Georgia, Middle

District of Arizona Charges 314 Individuals for Immigration-Related Criminal Conduct this Week
body: Press Release District of Arizona Charges 314 Individuals for Immigration-Related Criminal Conduct this Week Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Arizona PHOENIX, Ariz. – During the week of enforcement operations from Nov. 14 through Nov. 20, 2026, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Arizona brought immigration-related criminal charges against 314 individuals. Specifically, the United States filed 153 cases in which aliens illegally re-entered the United States, and the United States also charged 146 aliens for illegally entering the United States. In its ongoing effort to deter unlawful immigration, the United States filed 14 cases against 15 individuals responsible for smuggling illegal aliens into and within the District of Arizona. These cases were referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ICE-ERO), ICE- Homeland Security Investigations (ICE-HSI), U.S. Border Patrol, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF). Recent matters of interest include: United States v. James Allen Lynch. James Allen Lynch was charged by criminal complaint on Nov. 17, 2026, with Transportation of an Illegal Alien for Profit. On Nov. 16, Border Patrol Agents (BPAs) observed at least two suspected illegal aliens cross the United States/Mexico border. Approximately five minutes later, agents observed a solo driver, Lynch, in a Chevrolet Blazer traveling southbound toward the same location. Lynch was in the area for approximately five minutes before he was observed driving away. Agents followed and saw multiple occupants in the back seat ducking out of view. Agents activated their emergency equipment to conduct an immigration inspection. Lynch continued at a slow pace before yielding a quarter mile later. As agents approached the vehicle, three subjects wearing camouflage attempted to exit but were stopped by agents. Agents searched the vehicle and apprehended two additional subjects in the trunk area. The five subjects were determined to be citizens of Mexico, illegally present in the United States. [Case Number: 26-MJ-12624] U.S. v. Jesus Romero-Morales . On Nov. 19, 2026, Jesus Romero-Morales was charged by criminal complaint with Transportation of an Illegal Alien. On Nov. 18, a BPA in a marked vehicle was parked in the median of Interstate 40 (I-40) near Kingman, Arizona. The agent initiated an immigration inspection on Romero-Morales, who was driving a heavily tinted Ford Explorer. Inside the vehicle, the agent found five passengers, three of whom were citizens of China and two who were citizens of Mexico. All five were illegally present in the United States. The agent also learned that Romero-Rosales was a Mexican citizen without legal authority to be in the United States and that he had been paid to transport the aliens from Arizona to destinations in California. [Case Number: 26-MJ-01943] U.S. v. Carlos Yahir Moreno-Beltran. Carlos Yahir Moreno-Beltran was charged by criminal complaint on Nov. 19, 2026, for Transportation of an Illegal Alien. On Nov. 17, a BPA observed a Jeep Wrangler and a Dodge Ram truck driving in tandem northbound from a border construction area on South Avenue 25-East near Wellton, Arizona. The agent observed the vehicles separate at Old Highway 80, at which point the Jeep continued northbound before parking behind a barn. Upon seeing the BPA’s marked vehicle, multiple people were seen fleeing on foot from the Jeep. Another BPA located the Dodge Ram as it entered Interstate 8 heading eastbound. After the agent activated emergency lights to conduct an immigration stop, the driver of the truck, Moreno-Betran, accelerated and swerved on the roadway before crashing into another Border Patrol vehicle. Moreno-Beltran then led the BPA on a vehicle pursuit before agents used an immobilization device to bring him to a stop. Multiple occupants then fled from the truck. Additional agents responded to the area and ultimately apprehended 20 individuals. Emergency workers evaluated all 20 individuals for possible injury. Agents determined that four of the individuals were citizens of Mexico, four were citizens of Cuba, two were citizens of Colombia, one was a citizen of Ecuador, and one was a citizen of Guatemala. Agents further determined that all 20 individuals were illegally present in the United States. [Case Number 26-MJ-01942] A criminal complaint is a formal accusation of criminal conduct. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. title: Illegal alien charged with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship at DFW Airport
body: Press Release Illegal alien charged with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship at DFW Airport Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Texas Defendant entered the county dozens of times with fraudulently obtained U.S. passport FORT WORTH, Texas — United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould announced that an illegal alien from Mexico has been indicted for falsely claiming to be a U.S. Citizen after allegedly attempting to enter the country using a fraudulently obtained U.S. passport at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. On Nov. 18, a grand jury returned a two-count indictment charging Francisco Federico Reyes-Bravo, 45, for falsely and willfully claiming to be a U.S. citizen and misuse of a passport. “Falsely claiming U.S. citizenship is not a paperwork violation; it is a serious federal offense that threatens our national security and undermines the integrity of our immigration system,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “According to the allegations, the defendant repeatedly relied on a fraudulently obtained U.S. passport and another person's identity to evade lawful scrutiny to illegally enter the United States. My office will aggressively pursue anyone who circumvents U.S. law and compromises the security measures that protect the American people.” According to the criminal complaint, on Oct. 28, Reyes-Bravo arrived at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport aboard a flight from Veracruz, Mexico. He allegedly presented a United States passport bearing the name Javier Torres Rodriguez and claimed to be a U.S. citizen while seeking admission into the United States. The complaint alleges that during a secondary inspection conducted by U.S Customs and Border Protection officers, fingerprint analysis determined that the defendant was not a U.S. Citizen, but a Mexican national identified as Francisco Federico Reyes-Bravo with an active warrant issued by the Riverside County Sheriff’s Department in California. After being advised of his rights, the defendant admitted he was born in Ensenada, Baja California, Mexico. According to court documents, investigators determined that the U.S. passport presented by the defendant had been used to enter the United States 42 times through air and land ports of entry between 2018 and 2026. The complaint further alleges that the passport was obtained through the submission of fraudulent identity and citizenship documents, including a birth certificate and driver's license belonging to another individual. Reyes-Bravo is currently in federal custody. If convicted, the defendant faces a prison term of up to three years in federal prison for fraudulently claiming to be a U.S. Citizen and up to 10 years for misuse of a passport. U.S. Customs and Border Protection investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Connor Day from the Fort Worth Division is prosecuting the case. An indictment is merely an allegation, and all defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in a court of law. . ### Documents francisco_reyes_bravo_indictment.pdf reyes_bravo_complaint.pdf Contact Public Affairs Division U.S. Attorney’s Office Northern District of Texas USATXN.Media@usdoj.gov Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Immigration Component USAO - Texas, Northern

title: Hartford Man Sentenced to 6 Years in Federal Prison for Illegal Gun Possession
body: Press Release Hartford Man Sentenced to 6 Years in Federal Prison for Illegal Gun Possession Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Connecticut David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, announced that LAWRENCE SMALL, 33, of Hartford, was sentenced today by U.S. District Judge Kari A. Dooley in Bridgeport to 72 months of imprisonment and three years of supervised release for unlawfully possessing a firearm. According to court documents and statements made court, a state parole officer notified Hartford Police of an arrest warrant for Small, who had absconded from special parole.  In the early morning of March 30, 2025, Hartford Police identified Small as he left an apartment on Wethersfield Avenue and entered his car.  Small was forcibly removed from the car after he ignored officers’ demands.  A subsequent search of the vehicle revealed a loaded firearm with an extended magazine. Small’s criminal history includes felony convictions for robbery, assault, firearm, and escape offenses.  It is a violation of federal law for a person previously convicted of a felony offense to possess a firearm or ammunition that has moved in interstate or foreign commerce. Small has been detained since his arrest.  On July 31, 2026, he pleaded guilty to unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon. This matter was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and the Hartford Police Department.  The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney John T. Pierpont, Jr. Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Firearms Offenses Component USAO - Connecticut

title: Federal grand jury indicts Albion man for defrauding the VA out of hundreds of thousands of dollars
body: Press Release Federal grand jury indicts Albion man for defrauding the VA out of hundreds of thousands of dollars Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of New York BUFFALO, N.Y. - U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that a federal grand jury has returned an indictment charging Timmie L. Haynes, 64, of Albion, NY, with five counts of wire fraud, which carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. This action is part of the Trump Administration’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud. According to the indictment, Haynes served in the U.S. Army between December 4, 1979, and October 21, 1980, when he received a General Discharge Under Honorable Conditions. Shortly after being discharged, Haynes applied for Veterans Affairs (VA) disability benefits, which are monthly payments based on the severity of the disability rating, ranging from 0% (no compensation) to 100% (maximum compensation). Haynes claimed arthritis in his hand, wrist, knee joints, and lower back and was granted service-connected disability, but at a 0% compensation rating effective October 22, 1980. Haynes repeatedly sought increased compensation ratings, claiming progressively worsening joint conditions, eventually receiving a 100% rating effective October 31, 1989. Between 1991 and 1994, Haynes falsely claimed to the VA that he was wheelchair bound and presented himself as virtually immobile from the waist down. As a result of these false representations, on February 10, 1995, the VA granted Haynes Special Monthly Compensation (SMC), for loss of use of both of his legs. SMC is an additional benefit for veterans with severe service-connected disabilities. In addition, between 2004 and 2026, Haynes applied for and received funds from the VA’s Automobile Allowance and Special Adaptive Equipment Program, the Home Improvements and Structural Alterations Program, and the Veteran-Directed Care, to help with activities of daily living. During this time, Haynes also fought attempts to reduce his monthly benefit payment and discontinuance of his SMC after the VA received information that he no longer met the criteria to receive the benefit. In furtherance of his scheme to defraud, Haynes falsely represented to the VA that he was wheelchair bound, unable to walk, unable to use his left hand, and that he needed assistance with activities of daily living. In truth, from 1989 to the present, Haynes was not wheelchair bound and did not lack the use of his legs or left hand. Haynes could walk unassisted, drive without adaptive equipment, lift and carry objects, shop in stores without assistance, and perform other physical activities. As a result of his false representations, between 1989 and the present, Haynes received compensation and benefits totaling approximately $1,024,884.90. Haynes was arraigned before U.S. Magistrate Judge Jeremiah J. McCarthy and was released on conditions. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Paul E. Bonanno and Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Crystal R. Willis. The indictment is the result of an investigation by the Department of Veterans Affairs Office of Inspector, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Christopher F. Algieri, Northeast Field Office and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Allen D. Davis, II. The fact that a defendant has been charged with a crime is merely an accusation and the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty. # # # # Contact Barbara Burns 716-843-5817 Updated November 20, 2026 Topics Fraud Benefit Fraud Financial Fraud Component USAO - New York, Western

title: Attorney General Blanche Honors Goodyear Police Officer Dakota Berry for Distinguished Service
body: Press Release Attorney General Blanche Honors Goodyear Police Officer Dakota Berry for Distinguished Service Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Arizona WASHINGTON – Goodyear Police Officer Dakota Berry was among the law enforcement officers from around the nation who were selected to be honored by U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche today for Distinguished Service in Policing. This award represents the Department of Justice’s reaffirmed commitment to uplifting the valor and exceptional contributions to policing of our great nation’s law enforcement personnel. The Attorney General’s Honor the Honorable Award recognizes officers from state, local, Tribal or territorial law enforcement agencies for exceptional efforts in policing. The awarded officers, deputies, and troopers have demonstrated exceptional service in one of three areas: criminal investigations, field operations or exemplary community involvement. Within each category, awards were given to law enforcement officers and deputies who serve small, medium and large jurisdictions. Officer Berry was among the officers selected for the field operations category, which is intended to award those who have demonstrated exceptional bravery; heroic, quick, innovative, or otherwise exceptional problem-solving; and sustained excellence in achieving law enforcement goals, engaging in direct action to preserve life, or making a significant arrest. The Department of Justice award states, “In the early morning hours of May 25, 2025, Goodyear Police Officer Dakota Berry was returning to the city after completing a suspect booking when he encountered a catastrophic multivehicle collision. One vehicle was fully engulfed in flames. Trapped inside the burning car was a lone driver, frantically sounding the horn in a desperate plea for help. Without regard for his own safety, Officer Berry acted decisively and heroically. He broke the driver’s side window, reached into the inferno, and pulled the driver—whose hair was on fire—from the engulfed vehicle. Realizing the flames on the driver’s body were still active, Officer Berry immediately used his bare hands to extinguish the fire, sustaining significant burn injuries. After suppressing the flames on the victim, he located and used a fire extinguisher to eliminate the remaining fire on her person.” The award continues, “Thanks to his courageous actions, the victim—later identified as the daughter of a Goodyear firefighter—was transported in critical condition to a burn center, where she survived and continues to recover. Officer Berry also received treatment at a local burn center and made a full recovery from his injuries. The incident was captured in graphic detail by Officer Berry’s body-worn camera, drawing national attention and praise. Officer Berry’s quick thinking, fearless intervention, and unwavering dedication to duty unquestionably saved the woman’s life. His selfless courage, even in the face of immediate and life-threatening danger, reflects the highest ideals of policing and public service.” “Officer Berry represents the best of the best in bravery, selfless service, and community devotion,” said U.S. Attorney Timothy Courchaine. “Putting aside any thought for his own safety, Officer Berry ran toward danger to save a life. We are honored to have him serving here in Arizona.” “I was honored to recognize the very best of local law enforcement at the Department of Justice today,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “These men and women are playing a critical role in our effort to Make America Safe Again. The Trump Administration will never apologize for backing the blue and supporting local law enforcement.” “I am constantly mindful that even with all the resources available at the Department of Justice, it is local law enforcement who are on the front lines of making our country safe again,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward.  “The leadership of this Department of Justice never misses an opportunity to thank them for that.” The awardees for all categories were selected from a nationwide pool of nominees for their outstanding achievements and commitment to making American safe again. Nominations are now being accepted for next year’s ceremony and nomination information can be found here . More information about the awards can be found online: https://www.justice.gov/ag/policing-award RELEASE NUMBER:    2026-192_COPS Awards # # # For more information on the U.S. Attorney’s Office, District of Arizona, visit http://www.justice.gov/usao/az/ Follow the U.S. Attorney’s Office, District of Arizona, on Twitter @USAO_AZ for the latest news. Contact Public Affairs Esther J. Winne Telephone: (602) 514-7740 Esther.Winne@usdoj.gov Updated November 20, 2026 Component USAO - Arizona Press Release Number: 2026-192_COPS Awards

title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
body: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs NVIDIA and Microsoft expand tools for enterprises to customize AI models and deploy applications across cloud and local infrastructure. November 19, 2026 by Dave Salvator 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers , providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference. Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure. To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS . Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1 , Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1 , Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65. Helping Enterprises Customize and Deploy Open Models Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding the models and services available through Microsoft Foundry to help developers bring these capabilities into business applications. Microsoft’s serverless Programmed Training offering gives developers control over post-training workflows while Foundry manages the underlying infrastructure. Enterprises can focus on their business data, evaluating model responses and improving model behavior. Foundry Managed Compute adds support for deploying custom model weights, helping connect model customization with deployment through Microsoft’s managed services. EY used Programmed Training in Microsoft Foundry to adapt NVIDIA Nemotron open models for classifying corporate purchasing records, improving accuracy on its evaluation dataset by 55% and lowering cost by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models. The work demonstrates how enterprises can customize open models for specialized business tasks. The expanded NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 lineup on Foundry Managed Compute supports different requirements across enterprise applications. Nemotron 3.5 Super is designed for long-running agents working across coding, research and business workflows, while Lightning supports applications that need fast responses and tool use. Complementary models help agents find relevant information with Nemotron Embed and Rerank, extract structured information from documents with Nemotron Parse and detect harmful content with Nemotron Content Safety. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt — designed for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning — and Transcribe, for speech recognition, are coming soon. Bringing AI Closer to Enterprise Data NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding deployment options beyond the cloud, helping organizations run models and agents closer to their data while maintaining control over their infrastructure and operations. Expanded support for Nemotron 3.5 in Foundry Local brings capabilities for reasoning, coding and tool-using agents to Azure Local environments. Retrieval models help applications find evidence across text, document images, charts and tables. Azure Local will also support NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners, giving organizations additional options for deploying AI on premises. Azure Local is expanding to NVIDIA Jetson Thor and Jetson Orin edge AI platforms to support industrial applications such as machine vision, robotics and autonomous operations. NVIDIA physical AI models, including Cosmos , are also being brought to Foundry Local. On Windows PCs powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark , NVIDIA and Microsoft will showcase local large language model experiences at Ignite, demonstrating how developers can run AI applications directly on devices. For organizations using Cloud PCs, the companies are bringing Direct Stream capabilities to GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs. These capabilities support demanding graphics applications with up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second and low latency, even over challenging networks. A limited preview is open for sign-ups, with public preview planned for early 2027. Connecting Scientific AI With Microsoft Discovery For scientific research, NVIDIA BioNemo Agent Toolkit and NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit are expanding into the Microsoft Discovery catalog , bringing models for life sciences, drug discovery and materials and chemical science into Microsoft’s agentic research platform. BioNeMo Agent Toolkit helps scientists use natural language to run computational biology workflows in Microsoft Discovery, with agents coordinating the tools and model calls needed to carry out the work. An initial integration uses the RFD4-Proteina model , developed in collaboration with the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, to generate candidate protein structures and amino acid sequences for further evaluation and laboratory validation. Accelerating Microsoft’s Models and Services Alongside expanding customer access to NVIDIA technologies, Microsoft is using NVIDIA software and accelerated computing in its own AI development and services. Microsoft AI uses NVIDIA Dynamo to support reinforcement learning rollout inference during post-training. This computationally intensive process generates the experiences used to improve models. Dynamo coordinates inference across a large GPU fleet, optimizing performance, as well as helping manage requests, model updates and recovery from failures. The deployment builds on joint engineering between Microsoft AI and NVIDIA. Visit NVIDIA at Ignite for demonstrations spanning enterprise applications, robotics, accelerated data processing and local computing, with hardware including an NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 rack and RTX Spark devices. View NVIDIA sessions, hands-on labs and booth theater presentations . title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
body: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents See how developers are combining AI agents with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build simulation applications, test physical behavior and guide improvements. November 19, 2026 by NVIDIA Writers 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Your browser doesn't support HTML5 video. Here is a link to the video instead. Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Physical AI Paves the Path to Autonomous Industrial Operations 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Nyhamna_footage_take5_30s.mp4 AI agents powered by frontier models pave the way to autonomous operations. They use industrial tools and engineering data to help engineers build digital twins that test plans and processes and evaluate operational decisions. Falkor, a KONGSBERG company, shows how this works in practice. The company’s Falkor Surface platform lets customers turn their computer-aided design and engineering data into facility-scale digital twins using the GPT-6 Astra model. The platform uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition GPUs on Microsoft Azure to enable advanced physics simulation. AI agents built on Falkor’s agentic engine understand dense technical documentation, spatial relationships and real-world physics. Engineers can create and test plans in simulation before traveling on site, reducing costly delays and mistakes. They can also inspect equipment and check clearances in a shared view. Read Falkor’s article and watch the livestream f or a closer look at how the company builds these tools and checks the agents’ work. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗 Getting a robot model into a scene is only the start. Developers also need to assemble its components, add controls and check whether it can complete a task. NVIDIA developers Dillon Bailey and Rishabh Chadha used 3D assets from the SimReady Central library to build a pick-and-place simulation of a robot moving a can using the NVIDIA Isaac Sim framework. They directed an agent equipped with GPT-6 Sol and Isaac Sim skills to assemble the scene and generate pick-and-place controls. Testing the assembled scene shows how the assets work together, from joint movement and contact behavior to the gripper’s ability to hold, move and release the can. With that baseline in place, developers can adjust object positions and motion paths and repeat the tests to evaluate how each change affects the task. Follow the walkthrough to assemble and test a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim, with sample agent prompts and checks for robot movement and grasp behavior. Build a Voice-Controlled VR Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗 Bringing 3D assets into virtual reality (VR) requires more than rendering a scene. Objects need to respond to controllers and behave as expected when grabbed, moved or released. NVIDIA Omniverse community developer Michael Wagner took on this challenge. He directed GPT-6 Astra to use Blender software to model a study environment from two reference images, balancing visual quality with efficient performance in VR. He then used Claude Code to build an application that lets users find SimReady Central assets by voice and interact with them in an immersive VR scene. The Claude Code agent worked for about eight hours, and Wagner built the application over a weekend using an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada workstation and a Meta Quest 3 VR headset. The application ran on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries : ovstage shared the OpenUSD scene, ovrtx rendered it, ovxr enabled VR and ovphysx ran physics. Wagner later built a second version with ovnewton , which integrates with ovstage, to compare the physics libraries. The biggest challenge for Wagner was checking what happened inside the headset. Automated tests missed problems he could feel, including objects shaking when grabbed. Wagner reported the symptoms, guided the agent through changes and verified the interaction himself. Updating the grab control once per frame resolved the shaking. His takeaway: Give agents renders and logs to inspect, then check the experience directly. Explore his open source demo f or build instructions, a starting prompt and reusable agent skills. Send Microducks on Rounds in a Simulated Hospital 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/microducks-icu-pathtraced-16x9-1920x1080-1.mp4 Before adapting a robot to a new environment, developers need to test whether its walking policy — the AI that controls how it moves — can keep it stable in that setting. AI developer Maziyar Panahi directed Claude Code, using Claude Opus 5.5, to assemble an intensive care unit from 13 NVIDIA SimReady hospital assets and test Microduck robots inside it. The assets came with Newton physics settings, so Panahi didn’t have to model the furniture or create collision geometry from scratch. The Newton physics engine also helped replicate the ward so hundreds of copies could run together on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. When the cloud containers lacked graphics support, Panahi and the Claude Code agent separated simulation from rendering, recording robot poses in the cloud and rendering them locally. They also treated the furniture as static collision objects, which enabled larger runs within the solver’s limits. The robots walked using AI they had already been trained on and followed preset points along a route. Panahi checked how many robots remained upright: In a 256-ward run, 766 of 768 Microducks were still standing after 14 simulated seconds. He said the agent’s work took about two hours. Explore the open source demo for a starter prompt, checks and instructions to begin with one ward on a CPU, then scale to hundreds on an NVIDIA GPU. Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents 🔗 Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance. In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering. Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot_Hand_Video_Omniverse.mp4 Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools. These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications. Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill . Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗 Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Robotic_Dissasembly_Omniverse.mp4 PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model. Read Sensori’s story . Explore the Onshape importer guide. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab . Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗 Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial . Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗 Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗 Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗 A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab . Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial . Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

title: A smarter way to track and buy clean energy
body: A smarter way to track and buy clean energy Nov 19, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Granular certificates are a next-generation tool to ensure more accurate, impactful clean energy buying. Jenna Stauffer Head of Strategic Priorities, Climate Operations Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Read AI-generated summary We are advancing Granular Certificates to track clean energy by hour and location, providing clear pricing signals that encourage smarter grid management. These tools help you match electricity use with local clean energy production, supporting a more stable power system. You can watch our new video to learn how these certificates help developers, energy asset owners, and the grid. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We use Granular Certificates to track clean energy supply by specific hour and geographic location. Trading volume in the U.S. Mid-Atlantic region increased 437% during our recent monthly spot auctions. Our support for the Registry Acceleration Fund helps organizations verify and track hourly energy data. These certificates provide new revenue streams for battery storage operators and improve grid stability overall. We reduced our Scope 2 emissions by 3% while managing a 37% increase in electricity load. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are using new tools called Granular Certificates to track clean energy by the hour and location. These certificates help us match our electricity use with local solar or wind power, even when the sun is not shining. By creating clear price signals, this system encourages companies to build more batteries and clean energy projects where they are needed most. This helps us manage our power use and supports a cleaner, more stable energy grid. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Granular Certificates (GCs) are next-generation clean energy instruments. They precisely track supply by hour and location, helping companies match their electricity load with local clean energy. Their hourly pricing signals encourage the development of clean generation and energy storage when and where it is needed most. These instruments can incentivize improved grid management, and they can help accelerate the deployment of advanced clean technologies, leading to a cleaner, more stable power system. But like any nascent solution, the foundational building blocks need to be in place first. We first started piloting GCs in 2021 and, in just five years, they’ve transitioned from early concept to real-world certificates, traded on specific hours. We’re continuing to take actions to accelerate both our own procurement and the global GC ecosystem. Here are three key ways the GC ecosystem advanced this year: 1. The GC marketplace is growing. Marketplaces are critical because they establish transparent hourly pricing signals and help simplify processes for those new to hourly procurement. LevelTen, in partnership with the Granular Certificate Trading Alliance (GCTA) and the Intercontinental Exchange, launched the Granular Certificate Marketplace in the U.S. Mid-Atlantic grid region PJM in October 2025. Since that first auction, trading volume has increased 437% in just one year , with Google participating in every monthly spot auction. This increased trading volume generates clear pricing signals, with higher premiums occurring during evening hours. By demonstrating when buyers need clean energy most, GCs can incentivize suppliers to operate or build clean energy to meet this demand. 2. Global registries help with tracking and verification. Almost every corporate clean energy buyer uses registries, which track and verify their clean energy purchases via instruments like monthly or annual energy attribute certificates (EACs). Registries help also ensure EACs are not double counted, supporting unique clean energy claims. However, until recently, the vast majority of registries didn’t have the technical capabilities to accommodate GCs. To help address those gaps, Google supported the GCTA in establishing the Registry Acceleration Fund . The fund awarded grants to five of the largest organizations that operate registries, which collectively issue or track 4,000 TWh of certificates in over 70+ countries. As of today, one of these organizations has met their technical milestones that would allow them to transfer, verify, and retire GCs. The remaining four organizations are expected to finish in early 2027. This will add critical functionality needed for these instruments to scale, including standardization of the hourly data and traceability to one clear owner. 3. GCs are driving real value. Despite the GC market’s nascency, its potential benefits are moving from academic research concepts towards demonstrating real impact. For example, in a recent GCTA white paper , clean energy developers and asset operators shared real-life perspectives on granular matching. These developers explained that pricing signals from GCs can help them maximize existing energy assets in the near-term, while helping them make crucial decisions about project siting and technology diversification in the longer term. In addition, Google, esVolta, Quintrace, and LevelTen helped prove a new revenue stream for battery energy storage system operators. We partnered to pilot the first GCs for storage systems, shifting solar generation to match our targeted demand hours. This could not have happened without hourly tracking and verification via GCs. Hear more firsthand accounts of the benefits of GCs to developers, energy asset owners, and the grid in our new video . In addition to the maturing global ecosystem, we’ve also continued to evolve our use of GCs to help manage Google’s emissions. We’ll always prioritize applying new, long-term clean energy agreements, and the underlying hourly GCs, first. Even with a large clean energy portfolio, the sun doesn’t always shine and the wind doesn’t always blow exactly when we need it to. Marketplace GCs help fill those gaps. At the same time, our purchases help build a stronger market where GCs can be bought and sold quickly, easily, and in large quantities — creating clearer price signals and providing granular options for growing numbers of buyers. We used a smaller amount of marketplace GCs alongside a much larger amount of clean energy agreements to help lower our Scope 2 market-based emissions by 3% from 2024 to 2025 , despite a 37% electricity load increase. We will include a limited amount of marketplace GCs in our 24/7 CFE performance in the future. Looking ahead, these tools will become even more important to develop. The recently released net zero standard of the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) will require reporting on hourly matching performance for large energy users, and the GHG Protocol (GHGP) is evaluating the introduction of hourly emissions reporting. We will continue to work on developing and advancing GCs — not just for our own efforts, but to ensure others can use these tools to build a better energy system.
